title: Interpret the margin-of-error interval
subtitle: Inference from sample statistics and margin of error  · 11 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **11 of the official questions in Inference from sample statistics and margin of error  are this one** — 5 Easy, 5 Medium, 1 Hard.
It is bottom-heavy, which makes it cheap points. Secure it early.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- You're given an estimated mean or percent with an 'associated margin of error' and asked for the 'most appropriate/plausible conclusion' or the 'best interpretation'.
- The choices are sentences that mix 'between A and B', 'exactly X', 'greater/less than', or claims about ALL individual values or 'most' individuals.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Compute estimate − MOE and estimate + MOE.
- 2) Pick the choice that says the POPULATION mean or proportion (not individual values, and not the sample) is PLAUSIBLY between those two numbers.
- 3) Rule out any choice with 'exactly', 'not possible', 'every value' or 'all individuals', and any one-sided 'greater than' claim.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: It's two mental additions plus reading the wording carefully, and a graph gives you nothing here.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You apply the interval to individual values ('all handbags weigh between…', 'every visitor hiked…') instead of the population MEAN.
You pick a certainty word ('exactly', 'not possible').
You apply the interval to the sample instead of the population.
Or you misread MOE as the percent of respondents who were misclassified.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You apply the interval to individual values ('all handbags weigh between…', 'every visitor hiked…') instead of the population MEAN.
You pick a certainty word ('exactly', 'not possible').
